claims.text: Mg-containing lightweight HEAs can satisfy a density constraint below 6 g/cm³.
The as-cast starting alloy is a homogeneous, metastable, single-phase solid solution.
Rapid induction melting produces the proposed homogeneous non-equilibrium starting state.
Prolonged elevated-temperature exposure causes a metastable solid solution to partition into a precipitate-bearing matrix.
The partitioning specifically enriches magnesium in the precipitates.
The Mg-enriched precipitates are intermetallic compounds.
The Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates form preferentially along grain boundaries.
Prolonged corrosive exposure can itself drive the proposed Mg partitioning and precipitation.
Differences in constituent elemental properties drive diffusion and exsolution from the supersaturated matrix.
Mg-rich precipitates alter the local chemical potential near the matrix and grain boundaries.
Mg-rich precipitates disrupt the continuity and chemistry of the protective oxide or passive film.
Annealing at 800°C for 24 hours will measurably increase the Mg-rich precipitate volume fraction relative to the as-cast condition.
The post-treated material will have a higher corrosion current density than the as-cast baseline.
Precipitation-induced passive-film disruption is the cause of the increased corrosion current density.
The post-treated material will exhibit altered high-temperature oxidation weight-gain kinetics relative to the as-cast baseline.
Film disruption by Mg-rich precipitates causes reduced or spatially non-uniform oxide-layer formation.
Mg-containing Al-Cu-Si-Zn-Mg and Al-Mn-Zn-Mg-Si lightweight concentrated alloys have previously been induction-melted and heat-treated to obtain stable structures.
